html:
Cheikh Anta Diop was a Senegalese historian, anthropologist and physicist who argued that Africa stood at the centre of ancient history, and that ancient Egypt was a black African civilisation.

He studied in Paris after the Second World War. His book Nations nègres et culture (1954) argued that Egyptian language, culture and kingship were closely related to those of Africa south of the Sahara, and that Europeans had cut Egypt off from Africa to deny Africans a history. French academics resisted, and he only got his doctorate in 1960.

Back in Dakar he set up a radiocarbon dating laboratory, one of the first in Africa. He defended his views at a UNESCO conference in Cairo in 1974 and wrote for UNESCO's General History of Africa. He also led opposition parties against Léopold Sédar Senghor.

Many of his specific claims are disputed, but his challenge to European bias shaped Pan-African thought and later Afrocentrism. The university of Dakar now bears his name.
